msItem.title: Gospels (fragments)

msItem.note: Kephalaia (chapter list) of the Gospel of Matthew.
Gospel of Mark: preserving only Mk 1:1–3:34 and 6:21 to the end.
Kephalaia (chapter list) of the Gospel of Luke.
Gospel of John: preserving only Jn 6:14–8:3 and 15:24–19:6.
Prepared for liturgical use by an original hand. A part of the codex (99 folios) is preserved in Leningrad, GPB gr. 33. with most of the missing gospel text.

supportDesc.extent:
169 folios 295–300 235
III + 169 folios. Fols. I–III, 168 and 169 are paper flyleaves. The codex contains one inserted singleton, four paper bifolia, and 142 parchment bifolia.

collation.p: Greek majuscule quire signatures, written by the scribe, apparently separately for each Gospel, occur at the beginning of each quire on the recto, immediately beneath the last line of text near the outer right margin. Only two survive: Ε on fol. 92 and Η on fol. 116.

Collation: 1(1) 3 (ff. 2, 3, 4 = single leaves = fragmentary quires; 4) 8 (12; two quires missing before f. 5 and after f. 12) 4 (6–2: two leaves missing before f. 15, with loss of text; 16; three quires missing after f. 16) 8 (24; one quire missing after f. 24, probably with loss of text) 8 (ff. 25 and 32 = single leaves; 32) 3 × 8 (56) 2 (58) 2 (ff. 59 and 60 = single leaves; 60) 3 × 8 (84) 7 (8–1: one leaf missing before f. 91, without loss of text; 91) 5 × 8 (131) 11 (ff. 132–142 = damaged single leaves; 142; two quires missing after f. 142) 8 (150) 8 (158; several quires missing before f. 151 and after f. 158).

supportDesc.condition: Fols. 133–142 are shrunk by water and mounted in new parchment frames. There is water damage on many other leaves, but the remainder of the manuscript is in good condition

layoutDesc.layout:
Normally one column of 24 lines per page. Fols. 1r–1v and 60r–60v are written in two columns of 29 lines.
210 130–135 Ruling: Lake I, type 40c.
Fols. 1r–1v and 60r–60v. 215 115 Column width 70–75 mm. Ruling: Lake II, type 1e.

handDesc.handNote: The manuscript was copied by a single anonymous scribe in an upright ogival majuscule, slightly inclined to the left, with broad shaded strokes, in black ink. The Gospel text is written in this hand. The same scribe employed a smaller, more slender version of the script for the kephalaia lists, part of the liturgical annotations in the margins, and some numerals.

The same majuscule, executed in a narrower and smaller module in red and brownish-red ink, was used for the title of the Gospel of Mark, marginal kephalaia, part of the liturgical annotations, some marginal scholia, kephalaia, verse and canon numeration, numerals in the kephalaia lists, quire signatures, and the rubricated title of the Gospel of Luke. Numerous initials at or near the beginning of verses, some lightly ornamented, were likewise executed in this display hand.
Liturgical directions in dark-brown minuscule were added in the eleventh century or later, probably in the late Byzantine period. Breathings and accents were subsequently reinforced in a heavy hand.

decoDesc.decoNote: Ornamented headpieces occur at the beginning of the Gospels on ff. 17r and 61r.
Decorative closing bands occur at the end of the kephalaia lists and Gospels on ff. 1v, 59v, 60v, and 142v.
Numerous red initials occur at or near the beginning of verses; some are lightly ornamented.
Ecphonetic notation marks in red ink.

The ornamental headpiece at the beginning of the Gospel of Matthew survives in the St Petersburg portion of the codex (NLR, Gr. 33, f. 1), whereas that introducing the Gospel of John appears to be lost.

additions.p: Fol. 1v contains a Greek pen trial and an Arabic note (أذكرني يا رب إذا أتيت في ملكوتك) "Remember me, oh Lord, when you enter your kingdom".

binding.p: Brown leather binding; the cover is detached.

origin.note: The dating is based on Greek scribal notes in the manuscript: on f. 51v the note reads τελειοστα(ι) αγαπητ(οσ) ὁ χυρ(ι)ος Ματ(θαιος) ὁ εὐαγγελι(σ)της μην(ι) αὐγούστ(ω) ε̄, while on f. 99r it reads ἐτελείωθη ἡ δέτος αὐτὴ μηνὶ νοεμβρίῳ ξζ ινδ. η ἡμέρα ε̄, ὥρα β (nach Granström). Tischendorf proposed AD 844, but Crisci regarded this as impossible; other proposed dates are AD 889, AD 934 (Sobolevskij-Cereteli), and AD 979, the last being considered the most probable by Gardthausen and Crisci.

history.acquisition: Brought from the East by Tischendorf in 1853, and sold to the Bodleian for £125.
